hints: Focus on what a catalyst actually changes compared to what a temperature rise changes.
Notice the temperature is unchanged, so the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve, the average energy and the most probable energy all stay exactly the same.
Think about how a lower activation energy lets more of those same-energy particles succeed in each second.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a catalyst does**

Think of a catalyst as opening a shortcut, not as giving particles more energy. It provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy.

$$E_a(\text{catalysed}) < E_a(\text{uncatalysed})$$

**Check what stays the same**

Temperature controls particle energies, not the catalyst. Because temperature is unchanged, the average energy and the whole distribution of energies are unchanged.

**Link lower $E_a$ to rate**

With the same energies but a lower barrier to cross, a much larger fraction of collisions now have $E \ge E_a$. That means many more successful collisions happen every second, so the rate increases.

options.A: Incorrect. Average kinetic energy of particles is determined by temperature only. A catalyst at constant temperature does not heat particles up or increase their average energy.
options.B: Incorrect. The distribution of molecular energies (the shape of the Boltzmann distribution curve) depends only on temperature. A catalyst lowers $E_a$ but does not reshape the distribution.
options.C: Correct. By lowering activation energy, the catalyst increases the proportion of collisions that are successful. So a greater number of reactant particles react successfully per unit time, which is exactly what a faster rate means.
options.D: Incorrect. The most probable energy is the peak of the Boltzmann distribution and depends only on temperature. Since temperature is unchanged, the height and position of the peak are unchanged.
